prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

These items come from talks, interviews, threads, comments and advice, not only from papers. Some are advice the speaker gives or a view he argues for, not a decision his own team made. Write each of those as a decision point a research team faces ("A research team ..."), so that the advice or view is one possible resolution of it; the rules above apply unchanged. The text before the decision may be a transcript or a comment thread: use it only for the situation.

=== key 9fee2d7df7b1
Kind of decision: what evidence to collect
Problem: How to assess whether publishing a result could accelerate capabilities without bias.
Write-up text before the decision: To Mitigate Deceptive Alignment? Michaël: One thing people want to do is decrease the probability of deceptive alignment once we know that models are situationally aware. In your work, you mostly measure things like situational awareness. Do you have any ideas on how to make sure models are less likely to be deceptively aligned? Owain: I don’t have particular novel ideas. Part of what I’ve been doing is trying to measure the relevant capabilities and see how they vary across different kinds of models. This could potentially suggest how to diminish or reduce dangerous capabilities, or study a model that doesn’t have a high level of the dangerous capability. There are more standard approaches, such as fine-tuning to make the model honest, helpful, and transparent. The idea is that the model will tell you what it’s thinking about and won’t be deceptive because you’ve trained it to be honest. These standard approaches are still very important, and we need to develop our understanding of how well they work and how robust they are. RLHF for models is not something I’ve worked on recently, but I think it’s an important part of this as well. ⬆ Could Owain’s Research Accelerate Capabilities? Michaël: There’s a question from Max Kaufmann about whether some of your results, like on the reversal recurse, could lead to potential capabilities improvements. Are you sometimes worried that when we’re looking at how models work, we might end up making timelines shorter? Owain: Yeah, I’ve definitely thought about that. I’ve consulted with various people in the field to get their takes.

=== key d6e15e422e88
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Whether research on understanding models should be treated as a capabilities risk because it can improve model usefulness.
Write-up text before the decision: You don’t know why, but you did a big sweep and this architecture just works a bit better. Owain: How do I think about this overall? [...] The benefits of understanding the system better and some marginal improvement in usefulness of the systems ends up being a win for safety, so it’s worth publishing these things. If you don’t publish these things, it’s very hard for them to help with safety. The help might be pretty small. It might be different if you’re at a major lab and can share internally but not with the wider world. But even there, the best way to communicate things is to put them out there on the internet so people can have them at their fingertips. Michaël: There are two levels to what you’re saying. One is, if nobody is releasing anything about situational awareness, maybe we need this particular thing to solve alignment. In that case, we need to push capabilities forward a little bit anyway. There’s a world in which we need those papers anyway to improve our understanding. The other part is about being at a top AI lab. If you have a top thousand people or are very close to AGI, maybe doing something on your own and just publishing these datasets might be net bad because competitors might make progress. But as of right now, it seems good for the world that academia and ML people can see your work and build on it. Owain: Yes, that makes sense.
